title: The Mind in Daily Life
description: Ten essays, columns, an interview and a profile on everyday psychology: why we put things off, how habits form, the memory of smells, choice at the grocery store, first impressions, being bored, the end of a vacation, the fear of loss, the songs of our teenage years and how groups divide.

lessons.title: Why We Put Things Off
lessons.summary: A columnist looks at why we delay unpleasant tasks, when delay helps and how small steps and short sprints get the laundry done.
lessons.text:
There is a pile of laundry on the chair in my bedroom, and it has been there since Sunday. Washing it would take less time than writing this column. And yet, every evening, I look at the pile, feel a little frustrated with myself and find something else to do.

Most of us know the feeling. We put off the boring task and the difficult email, even though we know that the consequence of waiting will be worse than the task itself. Why?

Researchers now say that what we avoid is not the task but the bad feeling that comes with it. When a job seems overwhelming, the mind looks for quick relief, and a phone or a snack offers it at once. The relief lasts a few minutes; the consequence can last for weeks.

The result is a strange circle. The longer we wait, the bigger the task seems; the bigger it seems, the more overwhelming the feeling; and the more overwhelming the feeling, the longer we wait. Rarely does the task itself grow. Only our fear of it does.

Not all delay is bad, however. A little delay can even be beneficial: an idea that sits in the back of the mind for a few days often comes out better. A friend of mine, a writer, never starts an article on the day she receives it. First she takes a pencil and a notebook on long walks, and only then does she sit down to write.

The real problem, then, is the kind of delay that leaves us frustrated and anxious. For that kind, the most beneficial advice I have found is surprisingly simple: start small. Do not promise yourself the whole job; promise yourself five minutes. Once you have started, momentum does the rest.

Another trick is the short sprint. Set a clock for 20 minutes and work as hard as you can until it rings, the way a runner gives everything in a sprint and then rests. Twenty minutes feels possible in a way that a whole afternoon does not.

Will I stop putting things off permanently? Probably not. Some delay seems inevitable; humans prefer pleasure now to pleasure later. But if delay is inevitable, the guilt is not. Few habits change permanently overnight, but most can change a little at a time. Last night I took a pencil from my desk and wrote one line on a piece of paper: "Laundry, five minutes." Then I started. The laundry took an hour, of course, but I had my momentum, and the chair is finally empty.

Questions:
What has been on the chair in the writer's bedroom since Sunday?
A pile of laundry has been on the chair since Sunday.
According to researchers, what do we really avoid when we put things off?
We avoid the bad feeling that comes with a task, not the task itself.
How can a little delay be beneficial?
An idea that sits in the back of the mind for a few days often comes out better.
What does the writer's friend do before she writes an article?
She takes a pencil and a notebook on long walks first.
What is a sprint in the writer's advice?
It is 20 minutes of work as hard as you can, like a runner in a sprint, followed by a rest.
What did the writer do last night?
The writer wrote "Laundry, five minutes" on a piece of paper, started, and kept going thanks to momentum.

lessons.title: How a Habit Is Built
lessons.summary: An interview with a therapist who explains how habits form, why they are hard to change and how to build new ones.
lessons.text:
Dana Reyes is a therapist who helps people change their habits. We asked the therapist how habits form and how to build new ones.

What is a habit?

A habit is something we do without deciding to do it. Every habit has three parts. First there is a signal: a time, a place or a feeling. Then there is the action itself. Finally there is a reward, something that makes the brain want to repeat the action.

Can you give an example?

Many of my clients have a cookie habit. At 3 o'clock they feel tired at work. That is the signal. They walk to the kitchen and eat a cookie. That is the action. The sugar and the short break are the reward. After a few weeks their feet simply carry them to the kitchen. What they really want, though, is often not the cookie but the break.

Why is that pattern so strong?

Rewards stimulate the parts of the brain that deal with pleasure and learning. Repeat the pattern often enough, and the habit sets like cement. Wet cement can be shaped freely, but once it has dried, it keeps its form for years.

So is an old habit impossible to break?

Not at all, but it is rarely removed completely. It works far better to keep the signal and the reward and change the action. If what you want at 3 o'clock is a break, take a walk instead of eating a cookie. A walk will stimulate your body and your mind, and you still get your break.

What about building a good habit from nothing?

Start smaller than you think is necessary: not a book a week, but one page after dinner. It also helps to utilize a habit you already have as the signal: after I brush my teeth, I read one page. People who utilize their old habits in this way succeed far more often.

Some say that excellence is a habit, not a talent. Do you agree?

Partly. An old saying tells us that excellence is not a single act but something we do again and again. That means excellence is open to everyone, not just to the gifted. A musician's enhanced memory for music, for example, is built one practice at a time, until that enhanced skill feels natural.

How do your clients feel when a new habit starts to work?

Surprised, and then proud. People thrive on small results they can see. One client who had walked every afternoon for two months told me that she was sleeping nicely for the first time in years, and that the walk now fit nicely into her day.

Any final advice?

Be patient. Do not expect to thrive in a week; expect to improve a little each day.

Questions:
What does Dana Reyes do?
She is a therapist who helps people change their habits.
What are the three parts of every habit?
Every habit has a signal, an action and a reward.
What do many of Dana Reyes's clients really want when they eat a cookie at 3 o'clock?
They often want the break, not the cookie.
Why does she compare a habit to cement?
Wet cement can be shaped freely, but dry cement keeps its form for years, and an old habit is the same.
What does the saying about excellence mean to her?
It means excellence is open to everyone, because it comes from things we do again and again.

lessons.title: The Smell of Memory
lessons.summary: A writer explains why one smell from a hair salon carries her back to childhood, and what science says about smell and memory.
lessons.text:
Last week I walked past a hair salon, and the door was open. A warm smell of shampoo came out, and for a moment I was not in the city at all. I was 8 years old, sitting on a high chair in my aunt's salon on a Saturday morning, watching her cut a customer's hair and listening to the women laugh. I had not thought about that salon in 30 years. One breath of shampoo had transformed an ordinary Tuesday into a visit to my childhood.

Why does smell do this so much better than sight or sound? Information from the eyes and ears travels through several stations before it reaches the areas that handle memory and emotion. Smell takes a shorter road. It goes almost directly to those areas, which is why a smell often brings back not only a picture but a whole feeling, complete and sudden. Scientists have also found that these memories tend to be old ones, often from the first ten years of life.

Underneath almost every strong smell in my life, there is a place. The smell of diesel, for example, does not remind me of traffic. It reminds me of the old school bus that took us to my grandparents' ranch every summer. The bus smelled of diesel and warm seats the whole way. When I smell diesel at a gas station today, I still feel the same excitement I felt as a child on that bus.

The ranch itself had its own smells. In the mornings there was the rough bark of the tall pine trees, which smelled sweet after the night's rain; I still touch the bark of every pine I pass. In the evenings my grandmother cooked chili in a big pot, and the smell of chili filled the house long before dinner. My grandfather spent his evenings on the steps outside, breaking open nuts and giving me the best nut from each handful. Even now, the smell of a roasted nut takes me straight back to those steps.

Some smells are quieter. My grandmother dried the dishes with a clean cotton cloth that smelled of sun and soap. Years later, I found a similar cloth at a market, held it to my face and was transformed, for one second, into a child sitting underneath her kitchen table.

We cannot choose which smells will stay with us, but we can notice them. When a smell carries me somewhere, I no longer hurry past it. I stop, breathe and enjoy the journey. Last week, to the delight of the woman at the desk, I walked into that salon and booked an appointment, just for the smell. It was a small delight, but a real one.

Questions:
What happened when the writer walked past the hair salon?
The smell of shampoo carried her back to her aunt's salon when she was 8 years old.
Why does smell bring back memories so strongly?
Smell goes almost directly to the areas of the brain that handle memory and emotion.
What does the smell of diesel remind the writer of?
It reminds her of the old school bus that took her to her grandparents' ranch every summer.
What did the writer's grandmother cook in the evenings?
She cooked chili in a big pot.
What did the writer's grandfather give her?
He gave her the best nut from each handful.
What did the writer do last week?
She walked into the salon and booked an appointment, just for the smell.

lessons.title: Too Many Kinds of Jam
lessons.summary: An essay weighs the pleasure and the cost of endless choice at the grocery store, where every small decision tires the mind.
lessons.text:
A large grocery store sells a tremendous number of products, often more than 30,000. A single shelf may offer forty kinds of jam, sixty kinds of cereal and a lineup of soda in every color you can imagine. Yet many of us leave it feeling tired. Is so much choice a gift or a burden?

Psychologists describe a state they call decision fatigue. Every choice, however small, uses a little mental energy, and the supply is limited. Choosing between two kinds of soda takes almost nothing. But by the ninth or tenth small choice of the morning, the mind begins to slow down. Tired shoppers either pick whatever is closest or give up altogether and buy nothing.

A well-known study made this point with jam. On one day, a store offered free tastes from a lineup of 24 jams; on another day, from only six. The large lineup attracted more people, but the small one sold far more jam. Faced with too many options, many people decided not to decide.

Coupons, surprisingly, add to the problem. A coupon looks like a simple gift, but it brings new questions. Is the coupon for the large size or the small one? Is the product with the coupon still more expensive than the store's own brand? Each question is another decision, and by the end of the trip some people are so tired that they forget to use the coupon altogether.

Children feel this too. Ask a five-year-old to choose between fruit cocktail and apple slices, and the choice is quick. Show the same child a whole shelf of desserts, from fruit cocktail in glass jars to cookies in a hundred shapes, and the visit may end in tears.

Yet it would be wrong to conclude that choice is simply bad. People who lose a choice are often unhappy too. When a store stops selling someone's favorite soda, the complaints arrive quickly. Choice also allows people with allergies, special diets or limited budgets to find exactly what they need. What tires us is not choice itself but the need to make every choice again on every trip.

The most practical solution, therefore, lies somewhere in between. Shoppers who make their important choices once, at home, and write a list are rarely unhappy at the store. They walk past the tremendous lineup of soda without stopping, because the decision has already been made. Some people even buy the same breakfast every week, not because they lack imagination, but because they would rather save their energy for decisions that matter.

Not every decision deserves our full attention. Knowing which ones do may be the most useful choice of all.

Questions:
How many products does a large grocery store often sell?
It often sells more than 30,000 products.
What is decision fatigue?
It is the state in which the mind gets tired, often by the ninth or tenth small choice, because every choice uses a little mental energy.
What happened in the study with jam?
The lineup of 24 jams attracted more people, but the lineup of six sold far more jam.
Why do coupons add to the problem?
Each coupon brings new questions, and each question is another decision.
Why are people unhappy when a store stops selling a product?
They lose a choice they liked, such as their favorite soda.
How does a shopping list help?
The important choices are made once at home, so shoppers do not have to make them again at the store.

lessons.title: The First Glance
lessons.summary: A short essay on how we judge strangers in a fraction of a second, why that skill once helped us, and why a second look is worth it.
lessons.text:
Forming a first impression takes about a tenth of a second. A stranger walks into the room, and before he has said a word, we have already decided whether he seems friendly, clever or honest. In experiments, people who saw a face for only a glance made almost the same judgments as people who studied it for a full minute. More time did not change their opinion; it only made them more sure of it.

Why are we so quick? Historically, the answer is safety. For early humans, the fast detection of a hostile stranger could mean the difference between life and death. Someone who stopped to think carefully about every face would have been in danger. The brain therefore developed a system of rapid detection that works long before careful thought begins, and that system is still with us today, in offices, classrooms and job interviews.

What does this system look for? Mostly simple signals. An animated face, one that moves and reacts as we speak, tends to seem warm. A person who leans forward and gives a small nod while we talk seems to be listening, and we like them more for it. A nod costs nothing, yet it changes how the speaker feels. A calm, assured voice makes people seem capable, whether or not they are. And a red face with a vein standing out on the forehead looks hostile, even if the man has simply run up the stairs.

Here lies the problem. First impressions are fast, but they are often wrong, and once formed, they are surprisingly hard to change. In this way they work rather like an optical illusion. Most of us have seen the famous drawing of two lines that look different in length but are exactly the same. Even after you measure them with a ruler, the illusion does not disappear. An optical illusion keeps working, in other words, even after we know it is false. A first impression does the same: we keep seeing the assured stranger as capable and the quiet one as cold, long after the facts have told us otherwise.

In a similar vein, we feel more sympathy for people who look or sound like us. This sympathy is natural, but it is not always fair. The shy new colleague who barely spoke at the first meeting may turn out to be the most helpful person in the office.

Should we, then, ignore our first impressions? Not entirely. Sometimes a quick feeling notices something real, such as a warning in someone's voice. What we can do is treat the first glance as a first guess rather than a final answer. Only by giving people a second look do we see them as they are.

Questions:
How long does it take to form a first impression?
It takes about a tenth of a second.
Why did the brain develop rapid detection of strangers?
For early humans, the fast detection of a hostile stranger could mean the difference between life and death.
What kind of face tends to seem warm?
An animated face, one that moves and reacts as we speak, tends to seem warm.
Why is a first impression like an optical illusion?
It keeps working even after we know it is false.
Who do we feel more sympathy for?
We feel more sympathy for people who look or sound like us.
How should we treat the first glance?
We should treat it as a first guess rather than a final answer.

lessons.title: In Praise of Being Bored
lessons.summary: A columnist leaves her phone at home on the subway for a week and finds that being bored gives her mind room to wander.
lessons.text:
Look around any subway car in the morning, and you will see the same picture: almost every head is bent over a phone. Each small screen is a portal to endless news, games and videos. Thanks to that portal, nobody on the subway has to be bored for a single second anymore.

Historically, being bored was seen as a serious problem. Medieval writers described a heavy, restless feeling that came over people in the long, empty hours of the afternoon.

Today we have the cure in our pockets. The phone is always ready to entertain us. When one video ends, it shows a preview of the next before we have even decided whether we want it. The preview starts, we keep watching, and twenty minutes pass. The question is no longer how to entertain ourselves, but how often we should let the phone entertain us.

Some researchers believe the honest answer is: less often than we do. In one experiment, a group of people spent a quarter of an hour on a dull task, copying numbers from a list. Afterward, they were asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. The bored group came up with more ideas than a group that had skipped the dull task. Being bored, it seems, sends the mind wandering, and a wandering mind finds new paths.

I decided to test this on myself. For one week, I left my phone at home on my way to work. The first two days on the subway were hard. I read every sign in the car twice. I even caught myself trying to whistle quietly, until the woman next to me gave me a look, and I stopped.

By the third day, something changed. My mind began to wander, and it went to places it had not visited in months: an old friend I should call, a better way to arrange my kitchen, the first line of a story. I remembered being a child on rainy afternoons, when there was nothing to entertain me but a ruler and a pencil. I measured everything in the house with that ruler, and I would whistle as I worked. Those afternoons were not exciting, but they were full of ideas.

To be fair, being bored is not always useful. A person who is bored at work every day for years needs a new job, not a lesson in patience. But a few empty minutes on the subway are not a problem to be solved. They may be the only quiet room the mind has left.

My phone is back in my pocket now. Most mornings, though, it stays there.

Questions:
What do most people on the subway do in the morning?
They look at their phones, each a portal to endless news, games and videos.
How was being bored seen historically?
It was seen as a serious problem; medieval writers described it as a heavy, restless feeling in the long, empty hours of the afternoon.
What does a video app show when one video ends?
It shows a preview of the next video.
What happened in the experiment with the plastic cups?
The group that did a dull task first came up with more ideas than the other group.
What did the writer do on the subway when she was bored?
She read the signs twice and even tried to whistle.
What did she use to entertain herself as a child?
She used a ruler and a pencil.

lessons.title: Why the Last Day Matters Most
lessons.summary: An essay explains why we judge a vacation by its best moment and its end, using one family's trip to the coast as an example.
lessons.text:
Two summers ago, my family spent ten days on the coast. Eight of those days were glorious. The sun shone, the water was warm, and every evening we ate fish on a terrace above the harbor. On the ninth day, my son fell on the rocks and came back with a bleeding knee. On the tenth, our flight home was delayed by six hours. When friends asked about the trip afterward, my daughter described it in one word: tragic.

That was hardly fair. Eight glorious days against one bleeding knee and a long wait should add up to a very good vacation. But the mind does not add up experiences the way a calculator does. Psychologists have found that we judge an experience mainly by two moments: the best (or worst) one, and the end. They call this the peak-end rule. How long the experience lasted, and what happened in the middle, matters surprisingly little.

The rule appears almost everywhere. Ask people about a roller coaster, and they will describe the biggest drop and the final seconds, not the slow climb. In one famous medical study, patients remembered a long procedure as less unpleasant than a short one, simply because the long one ended more gently. Rarely does the length of an experience matter as much as the way it ends.

There is a second strange fact. Much of a vacation's pleasure comes before it begins. People report being happier in the weeks before a trip than in the weeks after it. The anticipated trip, full of imagined sunsets and quiet beaches, can be more enjoyable than the real one with its crowded buses. Planning, it turns out, is part of the pleasure, and the anticipated joy is real joy too.

What should a wise traveler do with this knowledge? First, protect the ending. A traveler who saves a special experience for the last day will have warmer memories of the whole trip. An old sailor I once met on a ferry put it simply: "Every sailor knows that you finish a voyage in calm water, not in a storm." Second, enjoy the planning.

Last summer, we tried this. We returned to the same coast, and on the final day we booked an aerial tour, a short flight in a small plane over the bays and islands we had explored. The aerial view was breathtaking, and my son, whose knee had long since healed, did not leave the window. The next morning, our flight was delayed again, by four hours. Nobody minded.

When friends asked about that trip, my daughter called it a triumph. In a sense she was right: it was a small triumph of good planning over bad luck.

Questions:
What happened on the ninth day of the first trip?
The writer's son fell on the rocks and came back with a bleeding knee, and later his sister called the trip tragic.
What is the peak-end rule?
It means we judge an experience mainly by its best or worst moment and by its end.
What do people remember about a roller coaster?
They remember the biggest drop and the final seconds.
Why can an anticipated trip be so enjoyable?
Much of a vacation's pleasure comes before it begins, while we plan and imagine it.
What advice did the old sailor give?
He said that every sailor finishes a voyage in calm water, not in a storm.
How did the family end their second trip?
They booked an aerial tour in a small plane on the final day.

lessons.title: Why Losing Hurts More
lessons.summary: An essay on loss aversion: why a loss feels stronger than an equal gain, where that caution helps us and where it costs us.
lessons.text:
Imagine that someone offers you a game. A coin is tossed: heads, you win 120 dollars; tails, you lose 100. On paper, the game is a good deal. Yet most people refuse it. Usually, the possible win has to be about twice as large as the possible loss before people agree to play. Losing, it seems, hurts roughly twice as much as winning pleases. Psychologists call this loss aversion.

A retired banker once explained to me how loss aversion looked from behind his desk. His clients, he said, would sell a stock that had gone up very quickly, to lock in the gain. But a stock that had fallen they kept for years, waiting for it to return to the price they had paid. Some of them checked every dividend as if it were a sign of hope, although a small dividend could never make up for the loss. "Selling it would have made the loss real," the banker said. "Keeping it allowed them to pretend."

Gambling shows the same pattern in a more dangerous form. A player who has lost money often keeps playing, not to win, but to win back what is gone. This is one reason gambling can be so hard to stop: each loss creates a new reason to continue.

We behave this way with objects too. A neighbor of mine keeps an old automobile in his garage. He has not driven it in three years. When I asked why he did not sell it, he said that no buyer would ever pay what the automobile was worth to him. Once something is ours, giving it up feels like a loss, even when it is only a car.

When two computing companies announced a merger last year, a friend who works in computing told me that her colleagues talked about nothing else for weeks. Very few of them discussed what the merger might bring. Instead, there was an outbreak of worry about what they might lose: their desks, their teams, their familiar routines. Like any outbreak, it spread quickly, even though in the end almost nobody lost a job.

Is loss aversion, then, simply a mistake? Not quite. For our early ancestors, a loss of food or shelter could mean death, while a gain usually meant a little more comfort. In that world, caution was a wise strategy. Even today, some caution protects us from bad deals and silly risks.

The trouble begins when caution grows larger than the danger. People stay in jobs they dislike, keep things they never use and refuse good offers, all to avoid the small pain of a loss. What helps is a simple question: if I did not already have this, would I choose it today?

Questions:
How much larger must a possible win usually be before people agree to play?
It usually has to be about twice as large as the possible loss.
Why did the banker's clients keep stocks that had fallen?
Selling them would have made the loss real.
Why can gambling be so hard to stop?
Each loss creates a new reason to continue, because the player wants to win back what is gone.
Why does the writer's neighbor keep his old automobile?
He believes no buyer would ever pay what the automobile is worth to him.
What did the workers talk about after the merger was announced?
There was an outbreak of worry about what they might lose.
When was caution a wise strategy?
It was wise for our early ancestors, for whom a loss of food or shelter could mean death.

lessons.title: The Songs That Stay
lessons.summary: A profile of a researcher who left physics for psychology and now studies why the songs of our teenage years stay with us for life.
lessons.text:
When Nora Feld enrolled in college 25 years ago, she planned to become a physicist. As a freshman, she spent her days on quantum theory and her nights listening to music. "I was obsessed with songs," she says, laughing. "I could tell you every word of a hundred of them, but I struggled with quantum physics." By the end of her freshman year, she had realized that the question she was really obsessed with was a different one: why do certain songs stay with us for the rest of our lives?

That question has filled her career. Today Dr. Feld teaches psychology, and she is known for a nationwide study of musical memory. Her team asked more than 10,000 adults across the country to name the songs that meant the most to them. The study was designed to include every demographic group: young and old, rich and poor, city and country. Across every demographic, the answer was surprisingly similar. Most people chose songs they had first heard between the ages of 12 and 22.

"The teenage years are when we decide who we are," Dr. Feld explains. "Everything feels important, and emotions are very strong. The brain stores the music of that time together with those emotions, almost like a soundtrack to the moment we became ourselves." That is why, she adds, adults who have not listened to the radio in decades can still sing every word of a song they loved at 15.

Her research also explains some familiar behavior. When a teenage idol from the past makes a comeback, adults rush to buy tickets, even if they do not know the singer's new songs. "They are not really buying a concert," she says. "They are buying a few hours with their younger selves." Every successful comeback tour, in her view, is a kind of time travel. Her own teenage idol, a singer she prefers not to name, made a comeback last year, and she went to the show twice.

The same research explains why older fans often dislike a remix. A remix keeps the words of a well-known song but changes its rhythm or sound. To a young listener, the remix may sound fresh. To someone who first heard the original at 16, it can feel as if a memory had been edited without permission.

Dr. Feld's first book, about music and memory, sold well. She is now writing a sequel, this time about the films we watch as children. "The sequel asks the same question in a different form," she says. "Why do some stories stay with us and others disappear?"

Does she regret leaving physics? She shakes her head. "Quantum theory was fascinating," she says. "But it never made me cry in the car."

Questions:
What did Nora Feld plan to become when she enrolled in college?
She planned to become a physicist.
What was she obsessed with as a freshman?
She was obsessed with songs and with why certain songs stay with us for life.
What did her nationwide study find?
Across every demographic, most people chose songs they had first heard between the ages of 12 and 22.
Why do adults buy tickets when a teenage idol makes a comeback?
They are buying a few hours with their younger selves.
Why do older fans often dislike a remix?
It can feel as if a memory had been edited without permission.
What is the sequel to her first book about?
It is about the films we watch as children.

lessons.title: Two Sides of the Park
lessons.summary: A columnist watches a township meeting about a dog park split into two angry groups, and sees how a trustee brings them back together.
lessons.text:
Our township is a quiet place of about 6,000 people, and its monthly meetings are usually quiet too. Last month was different. The only item on the list was a proposal to turn an empty field near the school into a dog park, and the hall was full before the meeting even began.

Within half an hour, the room had divided into two factions. One faction wanted the park; the other was against it. People who had waved to each other for years now sat on opposite sides of the room and refused to look at each other. Those who had arrived with mild opinions left with strong ones.

Psychologists have studied this behavior for decades. In some famous experiments, strangers were divided into groups for completely meaningless reasons, such as which of two paintings they preferred. Within minutes, people began to favor members of their own group and to judge the other group more severely. If a painting is enough to create a faction, a dog park is more than enough.

Once a group has formed, the ego joins it. Admitting that the other side has a good point starts to feel like a personal defeat. That is why so many arguments become petty. At our meeting, people argued about whether the grass would be cut on Tuesdays or Thursdays, about the color of the fence and about a dog that had barked at someone in 2019. None of these petty points was really the issue. Each was simply a way for one ego to win against another.

Then one of our township trustees, a retired teacher named Ruth Okoro, asked to speak. Before giving her opinion, she made a disclosure: her own house stood next to the field, so the decision would affect her more than most. Her disclosure changed the mood of the room. By admitting her personal interest openly, she showed that she was trying to be ethical, and people listened to her more carefully because of it.

The trustee then made an unusual suggestion. Before anyone argued again, each faction had to explain the other side's main worry, clearly enough that the other side agreed with the summary. It took twenty minutes. The parents worried about noise near the school; the dog owners worried about having nowhere safe to go. Once those worries were spoken out loud, the anger slowly left the room.

The final plan was a compromise: a smaller park at the far end of the field, with a tall fence and limited hours. Not everyone loved it, but everyone accepted it. The ethical behavior of one trustee had reminded us of an old virtue, the virtue of listening before answering. It is not an exciting virtue, but it may be the one a township needs most.

Questions:
What was the only item on the list at last month's meeting?
It was a proposal to turn an empty field near the school into a dog park.
What happened within half an hour?
The room divided into two factions, one for the park and one against it.
What did the famous experiments show?
Even strangers divided for meaningless reasons began to favor their own group.
Why do arguments become petty?
Once the ego joins a group, admitting that the other side has a good point feels like a defeat.
What disclosure did the trustee make?
She said that her own house stood next to the field.
What virtue did the meeting remind the writer of?
It reminded the writer of the virtue of listening before answering.
